newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan airline sets up China office.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan airline sets up China office.

text.p: Taiwan's China Airlines on Thursday confirmed it had set up a representative office in Beijing, but denied the move was intended to pressure Taipei into allowing direct links with China.
China Airlines spokesman Steve Yang said on state television that the Beijing office had been formed in June to handle the company's businesses in China.
"The office is handling things such as arranging flight transfers and issuing boarding passes for our passengers from Hong Kong (to China)," Yang said.
Taiwan has prohibited all direct links with China since a civil war separated the two sides in 1949. All flights must be routed through a third territory, usually Hong Kong, before arriving in China.
Yang said the office was not aimed at pushing Taiwan's government into opening up direct flights to China, but admitted such a move would be lucrative.
"The direct link question is an extremely political matter. Regardless of what operators may feel, we have to respect the government's policies towards the mainland," Yang said.
"Obviously (direct links with China) would have huge market potential."
Local media in Taiwan reported that several other Taiwanese airlines, including EVA Airways, were considering branches in China.

In July the head of China's state-owned flag carrier Air China toured Taiwan to explore cooperation with China Airlines and pave the way for direct air links. China Airlines had said it hoped contacts with Air China would improve its prospects for pioneering direct flights to the mainland.
Taiwan signed an air services accord with Hong Kong in June, which some analysts said effectively ended Taiwan's ban on direct transport links to China.

Under the pact, which required Beijing's tacit approval, China Airlines and Hong Kong's Cathay Pacific Airways will be able to continue flying lucrative Hong Hong-Taiwan routes after the British colony's return to Chinese rule in mid-1997.
The five-year deal also allows Hong Kong Dragon Airlines (Dragonair), in which Cathay Pacific has an 18 percent stake, to fly to Taiwan.

Pressure has mounted in recent years for Taiwan to lift the direct link ban. Taiwan investors, who have tendered for more than US$20 billion in Taiwan-funded projects in China, say the ban puts them at a competitive disadvantage.
